co_main_elk_crag.blurb: A bolted limestone cliff in the Main Elk Creek drainage above New Castle, and the busiest of the crags up the valley. Nearly everything here is sport, with a few trad lines mixed in, and the bulk of the climbing sits in the 5.11 and 5.12 range with a modest handful of 5.10s and easier. Velcro Glove, Pi and Gigantor are among the better-known lines. The wall sits in shade early and picks up sun later in the day, which makes cooler months the comfortable ones. Some starts go through loose, crumbly rock, so a helmet is wise, and on a pleasant weekend you may share the cliff with other parties.
co_main_elk_crag.parking_note: Drive Main Elk Road (County Road 243) about six miles from New Castle, to where the pavement ends and the road crosses the creek on a bridge. A big pullout just beyond the bridge, with a bulletin board, is the trailhead for Hadley Gulch.
co_main_elk_crag.approach: From the trailhead, follow the Hadley Gulch trail roughly a third of a mile to a signed junction for the 1840a trail. Go left through the gate in the fence and keep on the path for about half a mile to the creek. Follow the water briefly; the cliff rises on your right, reached by a steep, well-worn path.

co_dark_side_the.blurb: A long, curving band of dark, fluted limestone on Shelf Road outside Cañon City, and the shady option when the rest of Shelf is too hot. Almost all of it is sport climbing on hard, sometimes sharp rock, with a few trad lines, and the grades cluster from 5.10 through 5.12. The routes lean toward older-style bolting, so some lines ask for a few pieces of gear. Enchanted Porkfist, Blank Frank and Line of Strength are well-known lines here. Shade holds most of the day in summer, though the west end can see sun into midday; in winter it is the colder part of the canyon.
co_dark_side_the.parking_note: Use the day-use lot by The Bank campground on Shelf Road. Keep cars off the road itself.
co_dark_side_the.approach: Both ends start at the lot. For the west end, walk down the road toward The Bank, take the trail on the right soon after the road drops, and follow the base of the cliff band eastward with some scrambling. For the east end, walk back toward Cañon City about 100 yards to the turnoff for the group camp, follow the fence line to the rim, and downclimb a third-class chimney using the fixed rope.

co_rock_garden_climbs.blurb: A cluster of volcanic tuff formations up-canyon from the main walls of Penitente Canyon in the San Luis Valley. The rock is grippy and pocketed, with huecos, edges and crimps, and the climbing is mostly bolted face and corner routes with some trad and a few boulder problems. Grades lean toward the upper end, with most routes falling between 5.11 and 5.12 and a handful of 5.13s, though easier lines exist. Copacetic, The Reckoning, Court Jester and DOA are among the standouts. It is a quieter, more spread-out zone than the main canyon, so expect some walking between formations.

co_hawk_eagle_ridge.blurb: A quiet, shaded ridge on the south side of Eldorado Canyon that sees far fewer climbers than the famous walls. Nearly all of the routes are trad, with a few sport lines and top-rope options, and the grades are spread widely from easy through 5.13, with a decent share of 5.8 to 5.11. Rock quality varies, with some good stone mixed in with weaker sections, so the better lines are worth seeking out. Heart of Gold and Last of a Dying Breed are among the best-regarded. The walk in is steep and loose, so plan on a real effort to reach the base.
co_hawk_eagle_ridge.approach: The walk is steep and somewhat loose, taking roughly fifteen to twenty-five minutes. Start up the Wind Tower route, then continue on the East Slabs descent trail, climbing steep steps and working through a slot with some scrambling.

co_camp_bird_road.blurb: A backcountry winter zone in the hills above Ouray, with ice and mixed climbing along and just off a mining road. Mixed lines slightly outnumber the ice, with most ice at WI4 and the mixed mostly around M6, though both reach much harder. Skylight, The Ribbon, Bird Brain Boulevard and The Talisman are the famous names, ranging from short ice to long multi-pitch outings. The setting sits well above 10,000 feet, so expect cold, and slides can come off the slopes above the bigger ice routes, so check avalanche conditions. The rock is volcanic and can be crumbly with little natural protection, and mine traffic uses the road, so leave room for vehicles.
co_camp_bird_road.parking_note: Camp Bird Road leaves the highway south of Ouray. In winter it is usually plowed up to a gate near Senator Gulch, and climbers leave their cars beside it without blocking the road.
co_camp_bird_road.approach: From the gate, walk up the road, which brings most of the climbs within ten to fifteen minutes. The Skylight area is about half a mile on. For The Ribbon and Bird Brain Boulevard, drop into the main drainage and contour up to the base.

co_redgarden_s_buttress.blurb: The right-hand end of Redgarden Wall in Eldorado Canyon, with long routes on steep, polished stone. This is trad territory, and the grades are heavy in the 5.9 to 5.11 range with some 5.12s and a couple of 5.13s. Routefinding can be tricky and protection sparse, and the section has a reputation for serious, runout leads. Anthill Direct, Pansee Sauvage, Genesis and Desdichado are well-known lines. Many routes top out and walk off down the East Slabs, which feel exposed and slick when wet, while routes that end part-way use rappels.
co_redgarden_s_buttress.parking_note: Park near the entrance end of Eldorado Canyon State Park, then walk uphill a short way to the footbridge over the creek.

co_redgarden_tower_one.blurb: The pointed summit at the top of Redgarden Wall, with some of the longest and finest routes in Eldorado Canyon. It is a traditional area, with grades concentrated from 5.8 up through 5.12 and a few easier and harder lines. Ruper, The Yellow Spur, Vertigo, Super Slab and Grand Giraffe are all classics. The west-facing lines stay shaded until late morning, and popular routes can see queues, so start early. Plan the descent before leaving the ground, since the options (rappels or the exposed East Slabs scramble) are not obvious. Rattlesnakes are common near the stairs.
co_redgarden_tower_one.parking_note: Park near the entrance end of Eldorado Canyon State Park, then walk uphill a short way to the footbridge over the creek.
co_redgarden_tower_one.approach: After the bridge, continue upstream past the concrete pad. For Ruper through Super Slab, take the right fork near Tower Two. For Vertigo and routes to its left, take the left fork around the Pickpocket Wall and climb the Redgarden trail up the gully. The west face may need a short scramble to the ledges beneath The Yellow Spur.

co_penitente_entrance_area.blurb: The first walls you meet in Penitente Canyon, on both sides of the main trail in the San Luis Valley. The rock is welded volcanic tuff, grippy and featured with crimps, edges and huecos. Nearly all of it is bolted sport climbing, with a smaller number of trad lines and a single boulder problem. The grades run high, with most routes falling between 5.11 and 5.12, plus a number of 5.13s and a few easier ones. Colors of Emotion, Glutton for Punishment, Forbidden Fruit and Black is Beautiful are among the draws. Watch for snakes along the trail, and keep to the open paths.
co_penitente_entrance_area.approach: Follow the access road into the canyon, park in the lot, and take the single main trail in. The first routes start on the right after a short walk.
